     3	description: Use this skill for GPU training or inference clusters on SageMaker HyperPod (Slurm or

     5	  First, a GPU evidence coverage audit that proves per node whether kernel Xid logs and

     7	  found" is never reported from a silent log. Second, a node verdict (replace, reboot,

     15	metadata:
     16	  author: nzuresh
     17	  version: "1.0.3"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA, Chat tasks"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, AWS ParallelCluster, Amazon EC2, Amazon FSx for Lustre, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Amazon EKS, AWS Health"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Machine Learning, GenAI, High Performance Computing"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# GPU Cluster Evidence, Readiness, and Fault Verdicts
     24	
     25	For GPU clusters on SageMaker HyperPod (Slurm or EKS), AWS ParallelCluster, and self-managed
     26	EC2 or EKS. Generic investigation finds the obvious signals; this skill adds what it gets
     27	wrong: silent evidence, wrong-headline hardware verdicts, and predictable failures before a
     28	long run. **Read-only.** Never reboot, replace, update, or delete anything, and never read
     29	training data, checkpoints, or model weights.
     30	
     31	## Critical rules R1 to R10 (apply in every mode, in this order)
     32	
     33	R1. **Answer in one pass, and always leave room to answer.** In chat, do not stop to ask a
     34	   question and do not hand off to a separate investigation before answering. If an input is
     35	   missing, use the default (impact window: last 24 hours; run length: evaluate 24, 48, and
     36	   72 hours), state the assumption, and mark dependent checks `Needs input`. For "slow" or
     37	   performance questions with no time given, use the last 72 hours. Offer follow-ups only
     38	   after the answer.
     39	   **Budget the evidence gathering so the answer always gets written.** An investigation that
     40	   runs out of room before it reports is worth nothing to the operator, and it is worse than a
     41	   partial answer because it looks like a failure rather than a finding. So: collect the
     42	   mandatory evidence for the mode first (R2, R4, R5, and for Mode P the P1 to P6 core), then
     43	   write the report. Pick up the optional checks only with what is left. If you notice you are
     44	   deep into tool calls and have not yet produced an answer, **stop collecting and report what
     45	   you have**, marking everything unreached as `Not checked` with the call that would close
     46	   it. Never end a turn with evidence gathered and no verdict.
     47	R2. **Inventory and capability profile.** HyperPod: `sagemaker.DescribeCluster` and
     48	   `ListClusterNodes` (paginate). Read `NodeProvisioningMode` from `DescribeCluster`: if it is
     49	   `Continuous`, also pull `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` for the window (see rule R11), which
     50	   is the only timeline source that survives broken log delivery. On any other value the call
     51	   is unsupported and must be skipped, not retried.
     52	   EC2/ParallelCluster/EKS: `ec2.DescribeInstances`. For every
     53	   GPU instance type: `ec2.DescribeInstanceTypes` (strip HyperPod `ml.`): GPU count,
     54	   `EfaSupported`, `MaximumEfaInterfaces`; per EC2 node, attached `efa`/`efa-only` interfaces.
     55	   Report `<attached> of <max>`, where attached = interfaces with `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     56	   `efa-only` (the primary ENA interface does not count unless it is `efa`). HyperPod nodes
     57	   are not visible to `DescribeInstances`: say so. On NVSwitch types, search every log source
     58	   found under rule R4 for `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` before saying it is not confirmed.
     59	R3. **Node identity survives replacement.** A HyperPod reboot keeps the instance ID; a replace
     60	   gives the node a **new instance ID in the same instance group**, so the current ID will
     61	   never appear in the replace request. Query CloudTrail **by event name, not by instance
     62	   ID**: `cloudtrail.LookupEvents` with `LookupAttributes=[{AttributeKey: EventName,
     63	   AttributeValue: BatchReplaceClusterNodes}]`, then again for `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
     64	   `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, and `UpdateCluster`, with `StartTime` = window start minus 6
     65	   hours and `EndTime` = now as full ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, paginating with `NextToken`.
     66	   Keep events whose `requestParameters.clusterName` is this cluster. A `nodeIds` entry
     67	   that is not in the current `ListClusterNodes` output was replaced; the instance group
     68	   whose node has a `LaunchTime` just after that event is the replaced group. That operator
     69	   or automatic call is the explanation for the node going `Pending` (Branch E), not hardware.
     70	R4. **Find every log source by substring, not prefix.** Call `logs.DescribeLogGroups` with
     71	   `logGroupNamePattern` (case-sensitive substring) = the cluster name, then again for
     72	   `kernel`, `messages`, `syslog`, `journal`, and `gpu`, paginating with `nextToken`. Never
     73	   search only `/aws/parallelcluster` or `/aws/sagemaker` prefixes: customer pipelines use
     74	   other names (for example `/aws/<pipeline>/<cluster>/kernel`). Evaluate every source found.
     75	R5. **Prove coverage before any "no errors".** For each node and source: find the stream that
     76	   carries `kernel:` lines, then bin **that exact stream** by hour across the window padded by
     77	   one hour. **Always name the evidence you used: quote the full log group name and the exact
     78	   log stream name for every node in the coverage table, and again in the answer text.** A
     79	   coverage claim without the group and stream it rests on is not auditable, so the operator
     80	   cannot re-run it. Any empty hour means `Not observable` for that hour. First and last event times
     81	   are not proof, and the time of the **last `kernel:` line** is not when logging stopped:
     82	   a healthy kernel goes quiet. Liveness comes only from the hourly bins of all lines in
     83	   that stream. A node is `Measured` if one source passes. HyperPod: a missing
     84	   `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent/<group>/<instance-id>` stream means `No HMA detections`
     85	   when the cluster log group is otherwise live. NCCL transport with no `NCCL INFO` lines
     86	   anywhere is `Not observable`; never infer it from the instance type.
     87	R5a. **Name every resource you looked at, by ID.** A finding the operator cannot re-run is
     88	   not a finding. Whatever you analysed, put its identifier in the answer: the FSx file system
     89	   (`fs-...`) behind any storage claim, the instance IDs (`i-...`) behind any node claim, the
     90	   cluster name, the capacity reservation (`cr-...`) behind any capacity claim, and the log
     91	   group and stream behind any log claim as R5 already requires. "The file system was
     92	   saturated" or "the metrics looked fine" names nothing and cannot be checked. This applies
     93	   to the resource you cleared as much as the one you blamed, since ruling something out is
     94	   only useful if the reader knows what was ruled out.
     95	R6. **Verdict per node, headline to match.** `REPLACE`, `REBOOT`, `LEAVE ALONE`, `MONITOR`, or
     96	   `NOT OBSERVABLE`, against the evidence bar in `references/incident-branches.md` (Step 4b).
     97	   Application-class Xids (for example 13, 31) or HMA `reason: XidUserAppError` with the node
     98	   `Running` is `LEAVE ALONE`. Never headline "hardware error" unless the verdict is `REPLACE`
     99	   or `REBOOT` on hardware grounds.
     100	R7. **Label every cause** `Proven` (measured signal on the affected node, before the failure,
     101	   nothing competing) or `Hypothesis (to validate)` with the one confirming measurement. A
     102	   spike at the same time is correlation. FSx without a saturated metric is not a proven cause.
     103	   Only a `Proven` cause may be called the root cause, in the headline or in a branch table.
     104	   Otherwise write `Leading hypothesis: <cause>`, or `Root cause: Not observable` when the
     105	   deciding evidence is missing (for example a dead control-plane log). Never write "Proven
     106	   mechanism" for something whose trigger or removal path you did not observe.
     107	   Utilization metrics from FSx (`NetworkThroughputUtilization`, `DiskIopsUtilization`, and
     108	   similar) and `GPUPowerUtilization` are already percent from 0 to 100: a value of `0.9` is
     109	   0.9 percent. Quote the raw value with a percent sign.
     110	R8. **Recovery questions** always state three things: whether automatic node recovery is on
     111	   (`NodeRecovery`), what it does (reboot or replace the node), and that the **job** resumes
     112	   only with checkpoints plus the orchestrator's auto-resume (Slurm on HyperPod:
     113	   `srun --auto-resume=1`).
     114	R9. **Capacity Blocks** begin terminating instances 30 minutes before the end time (60 for
     115	   UltraServers); blocks end at 11:30 UTC and termination starts at 11:00 UTC on the last day.
     116	   For a planned run, write out: usable until = end time minus the lead time; run end = start
     117	   plus run length; hours covered = usable until minus start. Give every value as a full UTC
     118	   date and time, and check the latest safe start is not already in the past.
     119	R10. **Rule out the frequent non-GPU causes** in `references/cluster-edge-cases.md` before
     120	   blaming hardware: subnet IP or network interface exhaustion, ParallelCluster bootstrap
     121	   failures and protected mode, EFA nodes in a public subnet, a Capacity Block not yet
     122	   active, and the FSx maintenance window. HyperPod does not export system metrics to
     123	   CloudWatch, so HyperPod GPU activity is `Not observable` there.
     124	R11. **When the logs are dead, ask the control plane.** On a HyperPod cluster with
     125	   `NodeProvisioningMode = Continuous`, `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` gives you a node and
     126	   cluster timeline that owes nothing to a log agent, so it keeps answering when a stream has
     127	   gone silent or a node has disappeared. Filter the window with `EventTimeAfter` and
     128	   `EventTimeBefore`, narrow with `NodeId` or `InstanceGroupName`, sort with
     129	   `SortBy=EventTime`, and page through `NextToken`. Where a `Description` is not
     130	   self-explanatory, `DescribeClusterEvent` has the detail. Note that the response has no
     131	   severity or level field at all, so any grouping you apply is your own and should be
     132	   described that way. If `NodeProvisioningMode` is anything other than `Continuous` the call
     133	   is not supported; write `ListClusterEvents not supported` in the coverage table and carry
     134	   on. What you must not do is report a dead log as "no events" without either trying this
     135	   source or saying it was unavailable.
     136	
     137	## Pick the mode
     138	
     139	| The user asks | Mode | Steps to run |
     140	|---------------|------|--------------|
     141	| Something failed, hung, slowed, or lost nodes | **I: Incident** | Steps 1 to 7 |
     142	| "Were there GPU errors?", "Can I trust the logs?" | **C: Coverage audit** | Steps 1 to 3, then 6 and 7 |
     143	| "Is the cluster ready for a long run?", Capacity Block ending | **P: Pre-flight** | Steps 1 to 3, then 5P, 6 and 7 |
     144	
     145	## Workflow checklist
     146	
     147	Work through these in order and tick each one as it completes. Skip only the steps the
     148	mode table excludes. Every step below has a matching `## Step N` section with its detail.
     149	
     150	- [ ] Step 1: Scope the request: account, region, cluster or instance IDs, impact window
     151	- [ ] Step 2: Build the inventory, capability profile, and one ordered timeline
     152	- [ ] Step 3: Prove GPU log coverage per node before looking for errors
     153	- [ ] Step 4: Classify each fault and give every node a verdict
     154	- [ ] Step 5: Pull metrics and settle the root-cause branch
     155	- [ ] Step 5P: Score pre-flight checks P1 to P16 (Mode P only, replaces Steps 4 and 5)
     156	- [ ] Step 6: Write the report in the required format
     157	- [ ] Step 7: Self-check the finished output, then present it
     158	
     159	## Step 1: Scope
     160	
     161	Account, region, cluster name or instance IDs, workload, impact window (default last 24 hours,
     162	stated). Classify the symptom to pick a starting branch (Step 5), but collect evidence for all.
     163	
     164	## Step 2: Inventory and timeline
     165	
     166	Load [references/inventory-and-timeline.md](references/inventory-and-timeline.md) for the
     167	inventory API calls and the eight timeline sources, and
     168	[references/cluster-edge-cases.md](references/cluster-edge-cases.md) for the frequent non-GPU
     169	causes to rule out under rule R10:
     170	
     171	```
     172	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/inventory-and-timeline.md")
     173	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/cluster-edge-cases.md")
     174	```
     175	
     176	Build one ordered timeline for the window plus 30 minutes each side: node state, HMA
     177	detections, Xids, AWS Health, EC2 status and scheduled events, Capacity Block and training plan
     178	end times, and CloudTrail cluster changes (rule R3).
     179	
     180	## Step 3: Coverage audit
     181	
     182	Load [references/coverage-audit.md](references/coverage-audit.md) for the log-source discovery
     183	and hourly coverage queries, and
     184	[references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md](references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md) for NCCL transport, NVLink and
     185	NVSwitch, and EFA signals:
     186	
     187	```
     188	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/coverage-audit.md")
     189	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md")
     190	```
     191	
     192	Produce the coverage table and the node capability and fabric table for every affected node.
     193	Every row names the full log group name and the exact log stream name that row's verdict rests
     194	on, so the operator can re-run the same query. Where no stream carries kernel lines, say which
     195	groups you searched and that none did.
     196	
     197	## Step 4: Classify faults and give node verdicts
     198	
     199	Load [references/xid-triage.md](references/xid-triage.md) for the Xid catalog and per-code
     200	verdicts, and [references/incident-branches.md](references/incident-branches.md) for the node
     201	verdict evidence bar and branches A to F:
     202	
     203	```
     204	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/xid-triage.md")
     205	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/incident-branches.md")
     206	```
     207	
     208	## Step 5: Metrics and root-cause branch
     209	
     210	Load [references/signals-and-thresholds.md](references/signals-and-thresholds.md) for metric
     211	names, dimensions, and thresholds:
     212	
     213	```
     214	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/signals-and-thresholds.md")
     215	```
     216	
     217	Pull FSx (correct dimensions per metric), GPU activity (`AWS/EC2` `GPUPowerUtilization`, unit
     218	Percent, or `CWAgent`), and EFA counters, then evaluate branches A (hardware), B (capacity
     219	lifecycle), C (storage), D (NCCL, NVLink/NVSwitch, EFA), E (cluster change), and F (application,
     220	only after A to E are ruled out), as defined in `incident-branches.md`. Recommend operator
     221	actions only.
     222	
     223	## Step 5P: Pre-flight readiness (Mode P)
     224	
     225	Load [references/preflight.md](references/preflight.md) for pre-flight checks P1 to P16:
     226	
     227	```
     228	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/preflight.md")
     229	```
     230	
     231	Score checks P1 to P16. Lead with FAIL, then RISK. In Mode P this step replaces
     232	Steps 4 and 5.
     233	
     234	**Work the core first, then extend.** All sixteen checks together cost more tool calls than
     235	a single answer usually has room for, and a readiness question with no verdict is a failed
     236	answer however much evidence sits behind it (see R1). So run them in two passes.
     237	
     238	The core, which decides whether the run can start at all:
     239	
     240	| Check | Question it settles |
     241	|-------|---------------------|
     242	| P1 | Does the Capacity Block or training plan outlast the run? |
     243	| P2 | Is there an extension, if it does not? |
     244	| P3 | Is there a spare node to replace a failure? |
     245	| P4 | Is `NodeRecovery` on? |
     246	| P5 | Are deep health checks enabled? |
     247	| P6 | Is GPU error logging arriving, so a failure during the run is visible? |
     248	
     249	Write the readiness verdict as soon as those six are scored. P7 to P16 then refine it, and
     250	each one you reach can only add a `RISK`, never change a `FAIL` already found in the core.
     251	Anything you do not reach is reported `Not checked` with the call that would settle it, which
     252	is an honest answer; silence is not. If the core itself is incomplete, say which part and
     253	give the verdict you can support.
     254	
     255	## Step 6: Report
     256	
     257	Load [references/report-format.md](references/report-format.md) for the report template and its rules:
     258	
     259	```
     260	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/report-format.md")
     261	```
     262	
     263	## Step 7: Self-check before presenting
     264	
     265	Before showing the answer to the user, re-read your own draft and verify each of these.
     266	Fix the draft where a check fails; do not present an output that fails one.
     267	
     268	- [ ] Every "no errors found" statement is backed by a node whose coverage you proved in
     269	      Step 3. If coverage was not proven, the wording is `Not observable`, not healthy.
     270	- [ ] Every coverage row names its full log group and exact log stream (rule R5). A coverage
     271	      claim with no named source is not auditable and must be fixed before presenting.
     272	- [ ] Every node verdict still meets the evidence bar that justifies it, re-read from
     273	      [references/incident-branches.md](references/incident-branches.md) Step 4b.
     274	- [ ] The headline matches the verdicts. It does not say "hardware error" unless a verdict
     275	      is `REPLACE` or `REBOOT` on hardware grounds (rule R6).
     276	- [ ] Every cause carries a `Proven` or `Hypothesis (to validate)` label, and anything
     277	      labelled `Proven` has a measured signal on the affected node before the failure
     278	      (rule R7). Nothing unproven is called the root cause.
     279	- [ ] Every percentage came straight from the metric without rescaling (rule R7).
     280	- [ ] Every absent signal is reported as `Not observable` with what to collect, never as
     281	      zero or as healthy.
     282	- [ ] Each recommendation names an operator action, and no mutating API call was made.
     283	- [ ] Every number in the answer can be traced to a call you actually made this run.
     284	- [ ] Every resource you analysed appears by ID (rule R5a): the `fs-...` behind a storage
     285	      claim, the `i-...` behind a node claim, the `cr-...` behind a capacity claim, the
     286	      cluster name, the log group and stream. This holds for resources you cleared, not just
     287	      the one you blamed.
     288	- [ ] **There is an actual answer.** A verdict or root cause is written down, not just
     289	      evidence. If you ran out of room before finishing, the draft still leads with the
     290	      verdict you can support and marks the rest `Not checked` (rule R1).
     291	
     292	State the outcome of this self-check in one line, naming anything you could not verify.
     293	
     294	## Success criteria
     295	
     296	- Coverage table and node capability table for every affected node; no "no errors" without
     297	  proven coverage.
     298	- One verdict per node with a GPU signal; headline consistent with the verdicts.
     299	- Every cause labelled `Proven` or `Hypothesis (to validate)`.
     300	- Replaced nodes matched to the operator or automatic action that replaced them.
     301	- Mode P: P1 to P16 scored.
     302	- No mutating API call was made.

     85	## Event timeline (Step 3): Build the event timeline

     87	Pull all of these for the impact window ±30 minutes, then merge them into one ordered
     88	timeline:
     89	
     90	1. **GPU driver (NVRM) messages, from every log source that has them.** The NVIDIA
     91	   driver writes Xids to the OS system log as `NVRM: Xid (PCI:<bus-id>): <code>, ...`.
     92	   EC2 cannot see them from outside the instance, so they reach CloudWatch Logs only
     93	   if something on the node ships them. Find the source for the orchestrator (see
     94	   **Step 3a** below), then run this Logs Insights query against each source:
     95	
     96	   ```

     100	   | limit 200
     101	   ```
     102	
     103	   Extract per Xid: instance (from the stream name or message), code, PCI bus ID, and
     104	   first-occurrence time.
     105	
     106	2. **HyperPod health-monitoring agent (HMA) detections** (HyperPod only). Log group
     107	   `/aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<ClusterName>/<ClusterId>`, per-node log stream
     108	   `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent/<instance-group>/<instance-id>`:

     110	   ```
     111	   fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
     112	   | filter @message like /HealthMonitoringAgentDetectionEvent/
     113	   | sort @timestamp asc
     114	   ```
     115	
     116	   Extract per event: instance, `reason`, node condition (for example
     117	   `NvidiaErrorReboot`, `NvidiaErrorTerminate`), any `NVRM: Xid (...): <code>` text, and
     118	   DCGM policy violations (`"condition: ":"XID Error"` with `ErrNum`). HMA's own
     119	   `reason` is a strong classification signal: `XidHardwareFailure` points to Branch A,
     120	   while `XidUserAppError` means HMA judged the Xid application-caused and took no node
     121	   action, which points to Branch F.
     122	
     123	3. **Other HyperPod log streams** (HyperPod only) in the same log group, including
     124	   `LifecycleConfig/<instance-group>/<instance-id>` for lifecycle script failures on
     125	   replacement nodes, and any deep health check streams. Filter for `ERROR`, `FAIL`,

     135	   `system-reboot`, `system-maintenance`).

     137	6. **Capacity Block window.** For every capacity reservation with
     138	   `ReservationType = capacity-block`, add its `EndDate` to the timeline. EC2 begins
     139	   terminating instances in a Capacity Block 30 minutes before the end time for
     140	   instance types and 60 minutes before for UltraServer types, and emits a

     142	
     143	   For per-instance proof rather than a window inference, look for the
     144	   `Capacity Reservation Instance Interruption Warning` EventBridge event
     145	   (`source: aws.ec2`). Its detail carries `instance-id`, `instance-termination-time`,
     146	   and `instance-lifecycle: capacity-block`. That is the most direct evidence available

     149	   These events are only retrievable if the customer routes them to a target that
     150	   retains them (a log group, or an archive). If no such target exists, say the
     151	   per-instance warning was `Not observable` and fall back to the `EndDate` window,

     155	   `EventSource = sagemaker.amazonaws.com` for `UpdateCluster`,
     156	   `UpdateClusterSoftware`, `BatchReplaceClusterNodes`, `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
     157	   `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, and `StartClusterHealthCheck`; with
     158	   `EventSource = ec2.amazonaws.com` for `TerminateInstances`; and with
     159	   `EventSource = fsx.amazonaws.com` for `UpdateFileSystem`. Record who made the
     160	   change and when. If `LookupEvents` needs operator approval in this runtime, ask
     161	   once and continue without it if denied, and name the gap in the report.
     162	
     163	8. **HyperPod cluster events from the control plane** (HyperPod only, and only on

     178	   That is a capability limit, not an error worth retrying and not evidence about the

     186	                                                # EventTimeAfter / EventTimeBefore for the

     2	
     3	<!-- Loaded by SKILL.md. Content validated live against HyperPod Slurm, HyperPod EKS, and ParallelCluster clusters. -->
     4	
     5	## Step 4: Classify GPU and node faults
     6	
     7	Load the Xid reference before interpreting any Xid:
     8	
     9	```
     10	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/xid-triage.md")
     11	```
     12	
     13	For each Xid found (from any source in Step 3a):
     14	
     15	- Record the code, the node, the PCI bus ID, and the first occurrence time.
     16	- Use the reference to label it **hardware / node action**, **application**, or
     17	  **sympathetic** (secondary to another error).
     18	- If a hardware-class Xid on node N is the **first** error in the window and the job
     19	  failed after it, node N is the leading root-cause candidate.
     20	- If the only Xids are application-class (for example 13 or 31) and they appear on
     21	  many nodes at once, suspect the application or a bad input, not hardware.
     22	- Repeated hardware-class Xids on the **same** node across reboots mean that node
     23	  should be replaced, not rebooted.
     24	
     25	Also check the HMA event for `RepairAction` and `Recommendation` fields when present
     26	(for example `Recommendation: Please Replace the Faulty Node.`).
     27	
     28	## Step 4b: Node verdict (replace, reboot, or leave alone)
     29	
     30	Give every affected node exactly one verdict, with the evidence that meets its bar.
     31	Recommend actions only; never run them.
     32	
     33	| Verdict | Evidence bar (all must hold) |
     34	|---------|------------------------------|
     35	| `REPLACE` | Xid 64 or `Remapping Failure Occurred: Yes`; fewer GPUs than the instance type has; a hardware-class Xid that recurs on the same PCI bus ID after a reboot; Xid 79 or infoROM corruption that persists after a reboot; HMA `reason: XidHardwareFailure` with a replace recommendation or the EKS label `UnschedulablePendingReplacement` |
     36	| `REBOOT` | A first occurrence of a hardware-class Xid whose NVIDIA immediate action is a GPU reset or restart (46, 48, 62, 74, 79, 95, 109, 136, 140, 143, 158), infoROM corruption, a pending row remap, Xid 154 `GPU Reset Required` or `Node Reboot Required`, or the EKS label `UnschedulablePendingReboot`. No competing application explanation |
     37	| `LEAVE ALONE` | Driver configuration faults (Xid 119/120: deactivate GSP), node configuration or bootstrap failures, or only application-class Xids (for example 13, 31) that name a user process, or HMA `reason: XidUserAppError`, with node status `Running` and no hardware-class Xid. Hand the process name and PID to the application owner |
     38	| `MONITOR` | Informational or trend signals only (for example Xid 63, or 92 without escalation) |
     39	| `NOT OBSERVABLE` | The coverage audit (Step 3a) could not prove the node's GPU signals were arriving. No verdict can be given; say what to collect |
     40	
     41	State the verdict first in the report, then the evidence. If the user asked "should we
     42	replace the node?", the verdict is the answer.
     43	
     44	## Step 5: Collect storage and utilization metrics
     45	
     46	Load the thresholds reference:
     47	
     48	```
     49	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/signals-and-thresholds.md")
     50	```
     51	
     52	For each linked FSx for Lustre file system, pull `AWS/FSx` metrics with
     53	`cloudwatch.GetMetricData` at 1-minute period across the impact window. Use the correct
     54	dimensions; they differ by metric family:
     55	
     56	| Metric | Dimensions | Stat |
     57	|--------|-----------|------|
     58	| `DataReadBytes`, `DataWriteBytes`, `MetadataOperations`, `ClientConnections` | `FileSystemId` | Sum |
     59	| `NetworkThroughputUtilization`, `FileServerDiskThroughputUtilization` | `FileSystemId`, `FileServer` | Maximum |
     60	| `DiskIopsUtilization` | `FileSystemId`, `StorageTargetId` | Maximum |
     61	| `CPUUtilization` (metadata server) | `FileSystemId`, `FileServer` | Maximum |
     62	| `FreeDataStorageCapacity` | `FileSystemId`, `StorageTargetId` | Sum (and Minimum per OST) |
     63	
     64	Discover the valid `FileServer` and `StorageTargetId` values with
     65	`cloudwatch.ListMetrics` first; do not guess them.
     66	
     67	GPU activity signals, in order of preference:
     68	
     69	- `AWS/EC2` `GPUPowerUtilization`, dimensions `InstanceId` and `GpuId` (discover them with
     70	  `ListMetrics`). Published by EC2
     71	  itself for a subset of accelerated instance types with no agent. Unit is **Percent** of
     72	  maximum active power, so a value of `0.3` means 0.3 percent, not 30 percent.
     73	- `CWAgent` `nvidia_smi_utilization_gpu`, `nvidia_smi_memory_used`, and `nvidia_smi_memory_total`, if the customer runs
     74	  the CloudWatch agent with the NVIDIA plugin.
     75	
     76	Discover which exist with `cloudwatch.ListMetrics`. If neither exists, say GPU activity was
     77	not observable. Do not treat missing GPU metrics as zero utilization.
     78	
     79	**Idle reserved GPUs.** When the nodes run in a Capacity Block, training plan, or other
     80	reserved capacity, compute the hours in the window where every GPU on a node stayed below
     81	5 percent power utilization. Report them as idle reserved hours (a finding in its own right,
     82	because that capacity is already paid for) and use them as context: a job that was not
     83	running cannot have been slowed by storage.
     84	
     85	## Step 6: Decide the root-cause branch
     86	
     87	Evaluate every branch against the timeline. Report the branch whose evidence is on
     88	the affected nodes and precedes the failure. If two branches both have evidence,
     89	report both, with the order in which they happened.
     90	
     91	### Branch A: GPU / node hardware fault
     92	
     93	Evidence: HMA detection or hardware-class Xid on the affected node before the failure;
     94	node `InstanceStatus` `Failure`; EC2 status check failure; AWS Health hardware event.
     95	
     96	Then check recovery:
     97	
     98	- `NodeRecovery = None`: explains why no automatic replacement happened.
     99	- Node stuck in `Failure` or `Pending` for a long time with `CurrentCount < TargetCount`:
     100	  replacement is blocked. Check branch B (no capacity to replace into) and the
     101	  `LifecycleConfig` stream (lifecycle script failing on the replacement).
     102	- Node stuck in `DeepHealthCheckInProgress`: note that the documented DCGM level 4
     103	  diagnostic alone typically takes about 45 to 90 minutes. Only call it stuck well past
     104	  that range.
     105	- Job did not resume after replacement: check whether the job used auto-resume
     106	  (Slurm: `srun --auto-resume=1`) and whether checkpoints were written. The skill
     107	  cannot see this directly; ask the operator.
     108	
     109	### Branch B: capacity lifecycle
     110	
     111	Evidence: many nodes terminated within the same few minutes; that time is 30 minutes
     112	(instances) or 60 minutes (UltraServers) before a Capacity Block `EndDate`; or
     113	`CurrentCount < TargetCount` with replacements not launching and the Capacity Block
     114	or ODCR at `AvailableInstanceCount = 0`, or already `expired`. Capacity Blocks end at
     115	11:30 UTC, and termination of instances begins at 11:00 UTC on the final day, so a mass
     116	termination at about 11:00 UTC is a strong signature.
     117	
     118	A Capacity Block expiry is expected behavior, not a fault. The finding is the missing
     119	plan for it (no extension, no checkpoint before the end time, no alert on the
     120	expiration warning event).
     121	
     122	### Branch C: storage bottleneck (FSx for Lustre)
     123	
     124	Evidence during the slow or stalled period: `NetworkThroughputUtilization` or
     125	`FileServerDiskThroughputUtilization` near 100% on one or more file servers;
     126	`DiskIopsUtilization` near 100% on OSTs; metadata server `CPUUtilization` saturated
     127	with high `MetadataOperations`; or an OST with very low `FreeDataStorageCapacity`
     128	while others have space (imbalanced striping).
     129	
     130	Distinguish throughput-bound (large sequential checkpoint writes saturating network or
     131	disk throughput) from metadata-bound (many small files, high `MetadataOperations`,
     132	MDS CPU high, throughput well below capacity). The fix differs, so the report must say
     133	which one the metrics show. If no FSx metric is near saturation, say storage is
     134	**not saturated**. Do not recommend raising throughput when it isn't saturated. FSx does
     135	not publish client-side latency, so a metadata or I/O spike without saturation makes FSx a
     136	`Hypothesis (to validate)` as the cause of slowness, not a proven one. The confirming
     137	measurement is client-side: time a `stat` or small-file open on the mount during the slow
     138	period, or collect Lustre client metrics as described in
     139	[Best practices for monitoring FSx for Lustre clients](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/storage/best-practices-for-monitoring-amazon-fsx-for-lustre-clients-and-file-systems/).
     140	
     141	### Branch D: GPU communication (NCCL transport, NVLink / NVSwitch, EFA)
     142	
     143	Load the reference first:
     144	
     145	```
     146	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md")
     147	```
     148	
     149	Check four layers, each with its own evidence and its own `Not observable` state:
     150	
     151	1. **NCCL transport.** Search every log source for `NCCL INFO` / `NCCL WARN`. With NCCL
     152	   lines: EFA (`NET/OFI Selected Provider is efa`, `Using network AWS Libfabric`) versus
     153	   silent TCP fallback (`via NET/Socket/`), and NVLink peer access (`via P2P/CUMEM`,
     154	   `NVLS`) versus host memory (`via SHM/`). **With no NCCL lines, NCCL transport is
     155	   `Not observable`.** Never infer it from the instance type or the security group.
     156	2. **NVLink / NVSwitch fabric.** NVLink Xids (74, 71, 155, 156) on the affected nodes, and
     157	   on instance types the capability profile marks as NVSwitch, whether Fabric Manager
     158	   started (and, where the reference says so, found a usable CX bridge device). Exclude the benign systemd `PIDFile=` warning before counting
     159	   Fabric Manager problems. Non-Xid `NVRM:` NVLink lines are listed, not classified.
     160	3. **EFA counters.** `CWAgent` `efa_*` or HyperPod `node_amazonefa_*` retransmit, timeout,
     161	   impaired or unresponsive remote, and work-request error counts, compared with the hang
     162	   start.
     163	4. **EFA preconditions.** `ec2.DescribeSecurityGroups` on `DescribeCluster.VpcConfig` (or
     164	   the instances' groups): a self-referencing all-traffic rule inbound and outbound, as
     165	   EFA requires. Nodes of one job split across subnets or AZs. A failed HyperPod deep
     166	   health check (`InstanceStress` includes EFA loopback; `InstanceConnectivity` runs
     167	   multi-node NCCL `all_reduce`).
     168	
     169	A Branch D cause is `Proven` only with a signal from layers 1 to 3 on the affected nodes
     170	before the hang. A missing security group rule is a proven precondition failure. Everything
     171	else is `Hypothesis (to validate)`, and the report gives the NCCL collection command from
     172	the reference.
     173	
     174	### Branch E: cluster change
     175	
     176	A HyperPod replace (`BatchReplaceClusterNodes`, or `scontrol ... reason="Action:Replace"`)
     177	gives the node a new instance ID in the same instance group, and the node shows `Pending`
     178	until the replacement joins. Match the `nodeIds` in the CloudTrail request to the node's
     179	previous instance ID before treating the new instance as a different node. A reboot keeps
     180	the instance ID.
     181	
     182	Evidence: a CloudTrail `UpdateCluster`, `UpdateClusterSoftware`, `UpdateFileSystem`, or
     183	manual `Batch*ClusterNodes` call shortly before the failure; `CurrentImageId` differing
     184	from `DesiredImageId` (update in progress); nodes in `SystemUpdating`.
     185

{"id": "7d7ccadc-cd02-41df-90b7-d057739ce2d2", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_A6gJh9QulyKVQicbDWvf7z", "content": [{"text": "     1	# NCCL Transport, NVLink / NVSwitch, and EFA Signals
     2	
     3	Where each GPU-communication signal can be seen, what a good and a bad value look like,
     4	and what to do when it is not visible. Log strings are quoted from the sources linked in
     5	each section. Do not paraphrase them into search patterns that match more than they say.
     6	
     7	## 1. Which transport NCCL actually used
     8	
     9	NCCL writes its transport choices only when `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` (or higher) is set, and only
     10	to the job's stdout or to `NCCL_DEBUG_FILE`. These reach CloudWatch only if the customer
     11	ships job output. Search every log source found in SKILL.md Step 3a for `NCCL INFO` and
     12	`NCCL WARN` first. **If there are no NCCL lines at all, NCCL transport is `Not observable`.**
     13	Never infer "NCCL used EFA" from the instance type or the EFA security group.
     14	
     15	| Log line | Meaning | Verdict |
     16	|----------|---------|---------|
     17	| `NET/OFI Selected Provider is efa` and `Using network AWS Libfabric` | Inter-node traffic goes over EFA through the AWS OFI NCCL plugin | Good |
     18	| `Using network IB` | NCCL chose an InfiniBand-verbs network | Unexpected on EC2 EFA instances; report it |
     19	| Channel lines `... via NET/Socket/<n>` | Inter-node traffic over TCP sockets | **Bad** on EFA instances: silent fallback. The AWS blog on P3dn measured about a three-fold bus-bandwidth gain for EFA over TCP |
     20	| Channel lines `... via P2P/CUMEM` | Intra-node GPU to GPU by direct peer access (NVLink on NVSwitch nodes) | Good |
     21	| `NVLS Creating Multicast group ...` | NVLink SHARP in use for collectives | Good on NVSwitch systems that support it |
     22	| Channel lines `... via SHM/direct/direct` | Intra-node traffic through host shared memory | On an NVSwitch node, peer access is not being used; report as degraded |
     23	
     24	Sources: [NCCL logging](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/logging.html),
     25	[Training LLMs on SageMaker: best practices](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/training-large-language-models-on-amazon-sagemaker-best-practices/),
     26	[Optimizing deep learning on P3dn with EFA](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/optimizing-deep-learning-on-p3-and-p3dn-with-efa/).
     27	
     28	When NCCL is not observable, give the operator this to collect on one affected job:
     29	`NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET,P2P,SHM,NVLS NCCL_DEBUG_FILE=/fsx/nccl_%h_%p.log`
     30	(subsystem names from the NCCL logging page), then search the files for the lines above.
     31	
     32	## 2. NVLink and NVSwitch fabric
     33	
     34	The CloudWatch agent's NVIDIA plugin does **not** collect any NVLink counter (its full
     35	metric list is utilization, temperature, power, memory, PCIe link, encoder, and clocks).
     36	NVLink health reaches AWS only through the system log:
     37	
     38	| Signal | Where | Meaning |
     39	|--------|-------|---------|
     40	| `NVRM: Xid ...: 74` | Kernel log, HyperPod HMA | NVLink error (NVIDIA catalog: immediate action per NVLink workflow, investigatory action contact support). Hardware class |
     41	| `NVRM: Xid ...: 71`, `NVLink: fatal error detected on link <n>` | Kernel log, HyperPod HMA (`reason: XidHardwareFailure`) | Fatal NVLink error; example in the HyperPod HMA documentation. Hardware class |
     42	| `NVRM: Xid ...: 155` / `156` | Kernel log | GPU NVLink flit CRC error / lane error (listed by Amazon ECS GPU auto repair). Hardware class |
     43	| Other `NVRM:` lines that mention NVLink without `Xid` | Kernel log | Driver diagnostics. List them in the timeline with node and hour. **Do not classify** them or call them a cause without corroboration |
     44	| Fabric Manager start: `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` | System log (`/var/log/messages` or journal) | Fabric Manager service started. Applies to NVSwitch instance types (section 4) |
     45	| `CX Bridge device ... is usable for NVLink subnet management` | System log | P6-B200 and P6-B300 only: AWS documents that on these types Fabric Manager configures NVFabric through ConnectX bridge devices, so this line shows the bridge was found |
     46	| Fabric Manager absent, failed, or restarting on an NVSwitch instance | System log | NVLink between GPUs may not be up. Hardware or driver-stack problem: node verdict `REBOOT`, then `REPLACE` if it recurs. AWS documents Fabric Manager as required on P6-B200 and P6-B300; on other NVSwitch types, report a failure as a strong signal but label the NVLink impact `Hypothesis (to validate)` with `nvidia-smi topo -m` as the check |
     47	| `nvidia-fabricmanager.service: ... PIDFile= references a path below legacy directory /var/run/` | System log | systemd path warning. **Benign.** Exclude it before counting Fabric Manager "errors" |
     48	
     49	Sources: [NVIDIA Xid catalog](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/xid-errors/analyzing-xid-catalog.html),
     50	[HyperPod health monitoring](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-eks-resiliency-health-monitoring-agent.html),
     51	[ECS GPU auto repair Xid list](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/managed-instances-gpu-auto-repair.html),
     52	[EC2 public NVIDIA drivers, P6-B200 and P6-B300 considerations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/public-nvidia-driver.html),
     53	[CloudWatch agent NVIDIA metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Agent-NVIDIA-GPU.html).
     54	
     55	On-node confirmation for the operator (not available through AWS APIs): NVLink status and
     56	error counters from `nvidia-smi nvlink` and DCGM, and `systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager`.
     57	
     58	### On-node NVLink and fabric fields, captured from a live p6-b300.48xlarge
     59	
     60	Taken from a node running driver 595.91.07 and CUDA 13.2 with 8 x `NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC`.
     61	Quote these names as they appear. This is the operator-side evidence behind the NVLink 5
     62	family, Xid 144 to 150, in `references/xid-triage.md` rule 10.
     63	
     64	| Command | Healthy reading observed | How to read it |
     65	|---------|--------------------------|----------------|
     66	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -s` | `Link <n>: 53.125 GB/s` for every link | A link that is missing, or reads `<inactive>`, is down. Compare the link count across all 8 GPUs; an asymmetry is the fault location |
     67	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e` | All zero: `Malformed packet Errors`, `Buffer overrun Errors`, `Rx Errors`, `Rx remote Errors`, `Rx General Errors`, `Local link integrity Errors`, `Tx discards`, `Link recovery successful events`, `Link recovery failed events`, `Total link recovery events`, `Effective Errors`, `Symbol Errors` | These are the exact counter names on driver 595.91.07. Non-zero on one link on one GPU points at that link, and these are the counters to quote when an Xid 144 to 150 names a link. `Link recovery failed events` above zero is the strongest of them. Note the older `Replay Errors` / `Recovery Errors` / `CRC Errors` names are **not** present on this driver, so do not look for them |
     68	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e`, FEC fields | `FEC Errors - 0: <large and growing>`, buckets 1 to 15 at or near `0` | **Do not report bucket 0 as an error count.** It is the corrected-codeword counter and reads in the billions on a healthy link (36,140,749,276 observed at boot). Only buckets climbing above 0 indicate real link stress |
     69	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e`, BER fields | `Effective BER: 15e-255`, `Symbol BER: 15e-255` | `15e-255` is the floating-point floor, meaning effectively zero. Do not read it as a large exponent or a high error rate |
     70	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e`, raw lane fields | `Raw BER Lane 0: 2061`, `Raw BER Lane 1: 1038`, `Raw BER Total: 1037`, `Raw Errors Lane 0: 82`, `Raw Errors Lane 1: 4` | **All of these were non-zero on a healthy node at boot.** They are pre-correction physical-layer counters, so a non-zero value is normal and is not a fault. Never report `Raw Errors` or `Raw BER` as evidence of an NVLink problem on its own. Use them only as a trend against the same link's earlier reading, and lead with the corrected counters above |
     71	| `nvidia-smi -q`, `Fabric` section | `State: Completed`, `Status: Success`, `CliqueId: 0`, plus a per-GPU `GPU Fabric GUID` | `State` other than `Completed` or `Status` other than `Success` means the GPU has not joined the NVLink fabric. This is the single clearest fabric health field, better than parsing Fabric Manager log lines |
     72	| `systemctl is-active nvidia-fabricmanager` | `active` | Anything else on an NVSwitch type is a REBOOT candidate per the table above |
     73	| `nvidia-smi topo -m` | `NV18` between every GPU pair | `NV18` means 18 bonded NVLinks. A pair reading `SYS` or `PHB` instead has lost NVLink and fell back to PCIe or the host interconnect, which is the topology-level version of the SHM fallback in section 1 |
     74	
     75	Two things to watch for, both seen on the healthy node above. The FEC bucket-0 counter and
     76	the `15e-255` BER floor both look alarming at a glance and neither is a fault, so calling
     77	either one an error is simply wrong. Separately, `dmesg` on a healthy node carries
     78	`NVRM: API mismatch` warnings whenever a userspace component lags the kernel module
     79	version; `nvidia-gridd` did exactly that here. Filter those out before you count NVRM
     80	errors, the same way you would drop the Fabric Manager `PIDFile=` warning.
     81	
     82	## 3. EFA error counters
     83	
     84	| Source | Metric names |
     85	|--------|--------------|
     86	| CloudWatch agent `efa` section (namespace `CWAgent`) | `efa_retrans_pkts`, `efa_retrans_timeout_events`, `efa_impaired_remote_conn_events`, `efa_unresponsive_remote_events`, `efa_rx_dropped`, `efa_rdma_read_wr_err`, `efa_rdma_write_wr_err` |
     87	| HyperPod observability EFA exporter | `node_amazonefa_*` (for example `node_amazonefa_rx_drops`, `node_amazonefa_rdma_read_wr_err`) |
     88	| On the node | `rdma -p statistic show`, or `/sys/class/infiniband/<device>/ports/<port>/hw_counters/` |
     89	
     90	Read them as signals, not thresholds: a rise in retransmit timeouts, impaired or
     91	unresponsive remote events, or work-request errors on the affected nodes, starting at or
     92	before the hang, supports Branch D. A rise that starts after the hang is an effect.
     93	Sources: [CloudWatch agent EFA metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Agent-EFA.html),
     94	[Monitor an EFA](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-working-monitor.html).
     95	
     96	**Counting `/sys/class/infiniband` entries will not tell you whether EFA is attached.** A
     97	`p6-b300.48xlarge` launched with no EFA interface whatsoever still showed two InfiniBand
     98	devices, `ibp198s0f0` and `ibp199s0f0`. Those are ConnectX bridges, driven by `mlx5_ib` and
     99	`mlx5_core` on firmware `28.47.2526`, and they are how Fabric Manager handles NVLink subnet
     100	management on P6-B200 and P6-B300. The AWS public-driver page covers this, and it is the
     101	same hardware behind the `CX Bridge device ... is usable for NVLink subnet management` line
     102	in section 2. None of it is network fabric. On that node the `efa` kernel module was loaded
     103	but sat at a zero reference count, `/dev/infiniband` held only the ConnectX `uverbs` and
     104	`umad` pairs, and `DescribeInstances` showed no interface with `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     105	`efa-only`.
     106	
     107	On Blackwell, then, an InfiniBand device count tells you about the NVLink bridge and nothing
     108	about EFA. Reading two devices as two EFA adapters is a false positive waiting to happen.
     109	Count EFA the way rule R2 describes it, from `DescribeInstances` `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     110	`efa-only` measured against `MaximumEfaInterfaces`. If you want to confirm from the node,
     111	`fi_info -p efa` is the honest check, though it is missing from the base Deep Learning AMI
     112	until libfabric is installed. Failing that, look at which driver sits behind each InfiniBand
     113	entry instead of trusting the entry itself.
     114	
     115	## 4. Which instance types have an NVSwitch fabric
     116	
     117	`DescribeInstanceTypes` does not report NVSwitch or NVLink. Use the "GPU Peer to Peer"
     118	column of the [EC2 accelerated computing instance page](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/accelerated-computing/),
     119	summarised here as checked:
     120	
     121	| Instance types | GPU peer to peer | Treat as |
     122	|----------------|------------------|----------|
     123	| p4d.24xlarge, p4de.24xlarge | 600 GB/s NVSwitch | NVSwitch |
     124	| p5.48xlarge, p5e.48xlarge, p5en.48xlarge | 900 GB/s NVSwitch | NVSwitch |
     125	| p6-b200.48xlarge, p6-b300.48xlarge, P6e-GB200 UltraServers | 1800 GB/s NVSwitch | NVSwitch (P6e: NVLink domain spans the UltraServer) |
     126	| p5.4xlarge and other single-GPU sizes | N/A | No intra-node GPU communication |
     127	| Multi-GPU g7 and g7e sizes | Yes via PCIe | PCIe peer to peer, no NVSwitch |
     128	| Multi-GPU g4dn, g5, g6, g6e sizes | Not listed | `NVSwitch presence unverified`; do not expect Fabric Manager; the operator checks `nvidia-smi topo -m` |
     129	
     130	For a type not in this table, re-check the instance page. Never infer NVSwitch from the
     131	GPU model name.
     132	
     133	**The number in that table and the number `nvidia-smi` prints are not in the same units.**
     134	On a healthy `p6-b300.48xlarge`, `nvidia-smi topo -m` shows `NV18` between every GPU pair,
     135	meaning 18 bonded NVLinks, and `nvidia-smi nvlink -s` reports `53.125 GB/s` per link. Work
     136	that through and you get 956.25 GB/s in one direction, roughly half the 1800 GB/s listed
     137	above. Nothing is wrong: the published figure counts both directions, while `nvidia-smi`
     138	reports one. Divide one by the other and you will "discover" a half-width fabric on
     139	hardware that is fine. What actually matters is whether the link count and per-link rate
     140	match across the GPUs in the node. An asymmetry between GPUs is worth chasing; a gap
     141	against the published aggregate is not.
     142	
     143	## 5. Software stack minimums
     144	
     145	AWS publishes minimums for these types ([DLAMI P6 software requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dlami/latest/devguide/p6-support-dlami.html)):
     146	
     147	| Component | P6-B200 | P6-B300 | P6e-GB200 |
     148	|-----------|---------|---------|-----------|
     149	| NVIDIA driver | R570 | R580 | R570 |
     150	| NVLink 5 support | R570 | R580 | n/a in table |
     151	| CUDA toolkit | 12.8 | 13.0 | 12.8 |
     152	| Linux kernel | 6.1 | 6.1 | 6.12 |
     153	| EFA installer | 1.41.0 | 1.44.0 | 1.42.0 |
     154	| AWS OFI NCCL plugin | 1.15.0 | 1.17.1 | 1.15.0 |
     155	
     156	For other GPU types no minimum table was found. Compare with the stack of a current DLAMI
     157	that lists the type in `supported_ec2_instances` (DLAMI release notes) and report the
     158	result as a comparison, not a pass or fail.
     159	
     160	How to read versions without logging in:
     161	
     162	| Component | Where |
     163	|-----------|-------|
     164	| NVIDIA driver | Kernel boot line `NVRM: loading NVIDIA UNIX Open Kernel Module for x86_64 <version>` in the shipped kernel log |
     165	| Linux kernel | Kernel boot lines, if shipped |
     166	| AWS OFI NCCL plugin | NCCL INFO lines at init, if shipped |
     167	| CUDA toolkit, EFA installer | Not in AWS APIs; ask |
     168	
     169	A version that cannot be read is `UNVERIFIED`, not a pass."}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

Because FSx publishes no client-side latency and shows no saturation or load here, **storage on fs-077c776983688ad76 is neither proven nor even a viable hypothesis for the throughput slowdown** based on this data. Recommend the lead redirect to: which data path the B200 job actually used, and the GPU/NCCL/compute-side signals that ended ~Sep 23.

- **Relevant cluster**: AWS ParallelCluster `distributed-training-triage-b200` (Slurm, alinux2023, PC 3.16.0), tied to FSx `fs-077c776983688ad76` (tag Purpose=publishable-b200-fsx-benchmark).
- Head node: `i-01bbde10b04dd4ca8` (ip-10-0-1-24), us-west-2d, VPC `vpc-0028c20959269e96f`. Log streams for this head node (system-messages, clustermgtd, cfn-hup, clusterstatusmgtd) go **stale in late August 2026** — suggests cluster state moved on and a different/current head node may need to be identified.
- Older unrelated cluster `distributed-training-triage` (head node `i-08a11867e0b7e311d`) and two SageMaker HyperPod clusters (`skilltest-hp-slurm`, `skilltest-hp-eks-hp`) plus one EKS cluster (`skilltest-hp-eks`) created 2026-09-25 are NOT linked to this FSx — set aside.
- **GPU compute node inventory** (via CloudWatch GPUPowerUtilization InstanceId dimension, since live EC2 DescribeInstances shows none running):
  - 6 nodes tagged/expected as B200 (p6-b200.48xlarge, 8 GPUs each): `i-0a3cfc5c0505eb807`, `i-0190035035290b380`, `i-01ec042d2f0e3e7fb`, `i-0ce092c23d7562556`, `i-0be6193831c898671`, `i-0014ff22f2e2f180f`. These only have GPU activity data from **2026-09-23**, before the investigation window — not running training during the reported slowdown period.

# GPU Throughput Trend — `distributed-training-triage-b200` (account 111122223333, us-west-2)

## Headline finding
The six B200 nodes **never actually trained**. Across every node and every one of the 48 GPUs, `GPUPowerUtilization` peaks below **0.6%** and averages well under **0.2%** — the GPUs sat essentially idle the entire time they emitted metrics. There is **no throughput "decline"** to explain in the GPU layer, because the GPUs never ramped up. **The GPUs are not degraded; they are idle/waiting.** The bottleneck lies upstream (job never fed the GPUs — consistent with a storage/dataset or job-orchestration stall), not in the GPUs themselves.

## (1) Precise fleet active window (UTC)
The six nodes did **not** run as one synchronized fleet over "the last few days." They ran in **three disjoint, short cohorts, all on/around Sep 23–25, 2026** — not a continuous multi-day training run:

| Cohort | Instances | Active metric span (UTC) | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | i-0a3cfc5c0505eb807, i-0190035035290b380 | 2026-09-23 11:30 → 15:50 | ~4.3 h |
| B | i-01ec042d2f0e3e7fb, i-0ce092c23d7562556 | 2026-09-23 16:00 → 16:05 | ~5 min (2 data points) |
| C | i-0be6193831c898671, i-0014ff22f2e2f180f | 2026-09-23 16:20 → 2026-09-25 23:55 | ~2.3 days |

**Fleet envelope: 2026-09-23 11:30 → 2026-09-25 23:55 UTC**, but no instant has all six nodes simultaneously active. Cohort A was torn down (TerminateInstances at **2026-09-23 15:52:16Z** by the ParallelCluster HeadNode role, for i-0a3cfc5c0505eb807 and i-0190035035290b380) ~2 min after its metrics ended. No `GPUPowerUtilization` data exists anywhere between Aug 26 and Sep 23 — the Aug 27 RunInstances attempts **failed** (`Capacity Reservation cr-0884d02f8b1b344e5 is not active`).

## (2) Per-node table

| Instance | Cohort / active span (UTC) | Subnet / AZ | EFA attached-of-max | Instance type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| i-0a3cfc5c0505eb807 | A: 09-23 11:30→15:50; terminated 15:52:16 | subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb / us-west-2d | 8-of-8 (per launch template) | p6-b200.48xlarge |
| i-0190035035290b380 | A: 09-23 11:30→15:50; terminated 15:52:16 | subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb / us-west-2d | 8-of-8 | p6-b200.48xlarge |
| i-01ec042d2f0e3e7fb | B: 09-23 16:00→16:05 | subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb / us-west-2d | 8-of-8 | p6-b200.48xlarge |
| i-0ce092c23d7562556 | B: 09-23 16:00→16:05 | subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb / us-west-2d | 8-of-8 | p6-b200.48xlarge |
| i-0be6193831c898671 | C: 09-23 16:20→09-25 23:55 | subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb / us-west-2d | 8-of-8 | p6-b200.48xlarge |
| i-0014ff22f2e2f180f | C: 09-23 16:20→09-25 23:55 | subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb / us-west-2d | 8-of-8 | p6-b200.48xlarge |

Notes on EFA / type: terminated instances are purged from EC2, so per-instance NICs can't be described directly. Instance type and EFA count come from CloudTrail: launch template `distributed-training-triage-b200-gpu-p6b20048xlarge`, and a confirming (DryRun) RunInstances at 2026-09-23 15:51:32Z shows `instanceType: p6-b200.48xlarge` with **8 EFA interfaces** (`interfaceType: efa`, networkCardIndex 0–7), subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb, SG sg-0c6c57aa6bccdbb0d, capacity-block CR cr-0013d27d3b3d5dc3b. So **8-of-8 EFA, fully attached** — the network fabric was provisioned as expected; EFA under-attachment is NOT the problem.

## (3) GPU throughput-trend verdict

- **DECLINE: No meaningful decline — the GPUs never did work.** Cohorts A and B: max utilization **≤ 0.082%** on every GpuId. Cohort C (the only multi-day run, nodes i-0be6193831c898671 / i-0014ff22f2e2f180f): daily peak only **~0.58%**, daily average **~0.17–0.21%**. The headline "throughput dropped over the last few days" does not appear as a GPU-power decline because utilization was flat-at-near-zero throughout.
- **STRAGGLER: None.** On node i-0be6193831c898671 all 8 GpuIds are uniform (avg ~0.187–0.206%, peak ~0.54–0.58%); on i-0014ff22f2e2f180f all 8 are uniform (avg ~0.163–0.179%, peak ~0.48–0.52%). No single node and no single GpuId is persistently lower than its peers. There is **no slow/dead rank** bottlenecking a collective.
- **SYNCHRONIZED: Not applicable as a collective.** The nodes do not run together — they appear in three separate time cohorts, so they are neither collective-bound-busy nor independently busy. Within the one multi-day cohort (C), the two nodes track each other closely (both ~0.5% peak), but at idle levels.
- **IDLE HOURS: Essentially 100%.** Using the "<5% for the hour on every GPU" rule, **every hour across all six nodes qualifies as idle** — the fleet-wide maximum GpuId value ever observed is ~0.58%, two orders of magnitude below the 5% idle threshold. Cohorts A and B are entirely idle; cohort C is idle for its full ~2.3 days.

### Degraded vs idle
The GPUs are **idle/waiting, not degraded.** Hardware that was faulty would still typically show power draw (ECC retry loops, Xid-driven resets, stuck kernels). Instead power stays pinned near zero and uniformly across all 48 GPUs — the signature of GPUs that are **provisioned and healthy but never fed work**. Combined with the fully-attached 8-of-8 EFA fabric, this steers the root cause **away from GPU hardware and away from the network layer, toward the data path / job startup** (e.g., the FSx for Lustre `fs-077c776983688ad76` dataset read or the training job never progressing past input). That storage/data-path hypothesis is the right next thread to pull.

### Caveats
- Terminated instances are purged, so launch times and EFA are sourced from CloudTrail metadata (launch template + a DryRun RunInstances), not live `describe_instances`.
- The actual successful compute-node launches were issued by the ParallelCluster HeadNode role and do not expose the six instance IDs in CloudTrail `resources`; the metric spans above are the authoritative active-window bounds.
- Metrics for Sep 23–25 are at 300s resolution (within the 63-day window); 1-minute data has already aged out.

{"id": "c2dc23aa-5967-4951-883e-5557ef8186fb", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "The GPU trend data gives a decisive new picture: all 48 GPUs across the 6 nodes peaked below 0.6% power utilization, averaging under 0.2%, meaning they were essentially idle the whole time rather than training. I'm also seeing three disjoint cohorts, all clustered around Sep 23-25.

Cohort A ran ~4.3 hours before being terminated by the HeadNode role, cohort B lasted only about 5 minutes, and cohort C was the real main run spanning roughly 2.3 days. EFA was fully attached at 8-of-8 interfaces on the p6-b200.48xlarge instances, so the network fabric was provisioned correctly — that rules out EFA under-attachment as the culprit. GpuIds were uniform across the board too, so there's no straggler node. Earlier RunInstances attempts failed due to an inactive capacity reservation, but the actual cohorts ran under a different capacity-block reservation.

So I'm narrowing this down: storage is ruled out since FSx was idle, GPU hardware shows no Xid errors or stragglers (just idle, not degraded), and EFA was correctly provisioned though NCCL transport itself isn't directly observable from the logs.

The critical finding is that GPU power stayed below 0.6% for the entire 2.3-day run — the GPUs were essentially doing no compute despite the Slurm job showing as "running" with passing health checks. This points to the training being stalled somewhere upstream, but since FSx was also idle rather than saturated, I need to reconsider whether the bottleneck is really in the data path at all, or something else entirely blocking progress before the GPUs could even start.

If both GPUs and FSx sit idle while the job reports as running, the stall must be waiting on something else — not FSx throughput, not GPU compute. One strong candidate is an NCCL/network hang: a collective operation like all-reduce that never completes, leaving GPUs idle while waiting on a hung communication step, possibly due to an EFA or network fallback issue — though I'd expect the EFA attachment status to rule that out if it was fully attached.

Attached doesn't mean working, though — NCCL could still fail to use EFA due to misconfiguration and either fall back to slow TCP or hang outright, and that transport layer isn't visible from the logs. Another possibility is a slow, non-FSx data source like S3 reads or CPU-bound dataloading, but metadata operations were low too, so that seems less likely. There's also the possibility the job stalled at startup — stuck in rendezvous waiting for all ranks to join, or deadlocked before training even began. Let me reconsider the user's original framing about throughput dropping.

The GPU trend shows near-zero utilization the entire window, not a gradual decline, so the "drop" the user noticed is really the job stalling completely rather than slowing down — the timing is just when they happened to notice. With GPUs idle below 0.6% for over two days and FSx also idle, storage isn't the bottleneck in the saturation sense, but the combination of idle storage and idle GPUs together points toward something else entirely stalling the pipeline.

I don't see GPU hardware faults either — no Xid errors, no stragglers. EFA is fully attached across all 8 interfaces, but NCCL transport activity isn't directly observable from what I have. The still-running gpu-health-slurm subagent should be decisive here: if it shows the job hung at NCCL initialization or a collective operation, or shows GPUs with 0% SM utilization despite allocated memory, that would confirm this is a network/communication stall rather than a storage or hardware issue.

Idle GPUs with near-zero power draw for over two days while a job is marked as scheduled strongly points to a hang, most likely an NCCL collective hang where GPUs block on an all-reduce that never completes. But I should also consider whether the "job" was actually just Slurm health checks completing successfully rather than real training workload ever being submitted.

I'm narrowing this down to a few candidates: a network/communication hang, a dataloader stall unrelated to FSx, no real training job ever running (just orchestration-level health checks), or degraded inter-node communication where NCCL falls back to slow TCP instead of EFA. The gpu-health-slurm subagent result should settle which of these it actually is, so I'll wait on that.

While waiting, I'm also considering a backup path in case that subagent fails to surface throughput data, since the user specifically wants storage, network, and GPU causes clearly distinguished.

NCCL debug logs aren't shipped, so I need to check EFA counters directly, but the observability agent install reportedly failed, so those metrics may be missing too. I should check the security group for the self-referencing all-traffic rule EFA requires between the two nodes, since its absence would block collective communication entirely.

{"type": "finding", "id": "finding-gpus-idle-not-degraded", "title": "GPUs were idle/unfed, not hardware-degraded or network-bottlenecked", "description": "Across all 6 B200 nodes and all 48 GPUs, GPUPowerUtilization never exceeded ~0.6% in any of the fleet's 3 disjoint active cohorts (Cohort A: 09-23 11:30-15:50, 2 nodes; Cohort B: 09-23 16:00-16:05, 2 nodes; Cohort C: 09-23 16:20 to 09-25 23:55, 2 nodes -- the only multi-day run and the confirmed Slurm job). Per-GPU breakdown shows uniform near-zero values across all 8 GpuIds on every node (no straggler/outlier pattern), ruling out a single faulty GPU or thermal throttle as cause. CloudTrail confirms the launch template specified 8-of-8 EFA interfaces attached (p6-b200.48xlarge), so missing EFA/network fabric is not the explanation either. Kernel logs show healthy, continuous NVRM activity with no Xid errors, no ECC/throttle/remap events (only a benign NVLink inband-data diagnostic and a Fabric Manager service enable/start recipe re-emission, neither indicative of failure). However, DCGM/nvidia-smi telemetry, NCCL transport logging, and training-throughput metrics were never shipped to CloudWatch at all -- so GPU straggler/throttle/PCIe degradation and NCCL EFA-vs-TCP-fallback remain formally unconfirmed, not just ruled out. The pattern (uniformly near-zero power draw with healthy available drivers, confirmed EFA attachment) is most consistent with GPUs that are provisioned and functioning but never issued real training kernels -- pointing to the training job/data pipeline failing to progress (e.g., stalled on dataset load, orchestration failure, or job never truly starting) rather than a GPU hardware or EFA/NCCL network fault, though this remains a hypothesis given the telemetry gaps.", "supporting_observations": ["obs-active-gpu-node-idle", "obs-gpu-fleet-idle-during-training", "obs-uniform-gpu-idleness-no-straggler", "obs-per-node-metric-span-mismatch", "obs-efa-launch-template-config", "obs-benign-nvlink-fm-diagnostics"], "related_resources": ["i-0be6193831c898671", "i-0014ff22f2e2f180f"], "finding_type": "hypothesis", "deeplinks": []}

{"type": "investigation_gap", "id": "gap-gpu-health-slurm-log-coverage", "title": "gpu-health and slurm log groups lack data for active training nodes", "description": "Final confirmed state: the gpu-health log group contains zero records for either active training node (i-0be6193831c898671, i-0014ff22f2e2f180f) in both the base and -cf-test-v2 sibling groups -- the only stream present is an unrelated stale prolog event from a different node. The slurm log group contains only ParallelCluster HealthCheckManager plugin noise (280 records), with no steps/sec, tokens/sec, loss, or epoch data. No NCCL INFO/WARN lines exist in gpu-health, slurm, kernel, or the parallelcluster log group (119,240 records scanned) -- so EFA vs TCP vs SHM transport cannot be determined. No Fabric Manager 'Started' or 'CX Bridge usable for NVLink' confirmation lines exist either, so clean fabric bring-up cannot be positively confirmed (though no FM failure is observed). The kernel log group IS continuously live for both active nodes with no gaps, and shows no Xid, ECC, remapped-row, or throttle events -- this is the one trustworthy 'no hardware fault observed' signal, backed by proven continuous coverage. To close this gap: enable DCGM/nvidia-smi CloudWatch agent telemetry, rerun a job with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shipped to logs, and ship trainer stdout throughput metrics."}

{"type": "investigation_gap", "id": "gap-observability-agent-failure", "title": "Training observability agent failed to install on compute nodes", "description": "Confirmed definitively: CWAgent namespace in CloudWatch contains ONLY basic disk_used_percent and mem_used_percent metrics for the old head node i-08a11867e0b7e311d -- no nvidia_smi_*, efa_*, or any GPU/network performance counters exist for ANY node in the account, including the two active training nodes (i-0be6193831c898671, i-0014ff22f2e2f180f). This confirms the install-observability.sh bootstrap failure (rc=3) left the fleet with zero DCGM, NCCL, EFA-retransmit, or training-throughput telemetry for the entire investigation. Combined with the gpu-health/slurm log gaps, this means GPU straggler/throttle/PCIe degradation and NCCL EFA-vs-TCP transport can never be confirmed or ruled out from existing telemetry for this run -- only inferred indirectly (uniform near-zero GPU power draw, healthy kernel logs, correct EFA/security-group provisioning)."}

{"id": "6b4928a5-ded7-489e-8cf3-12b8c23a8118", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "I notice that CWAgent only has basic disk/memory metrics for this instance, which is actually the head node of the other distributed-training-triage cluster, not the b200 one — there's no GPU utilization/clock/temp/power data from the NVIDIA plugin, and no EFA network counters either.

This confirms the telemetry gap: the CloudWatch agent's NVIDIA and EFA plugins were never collecting data on the B200 compute nodes, consistent with the install-observability.sh failure. So I've now exhausted all available CloudWatch sources — FSx shows storage isn't saturated, GPUPowerUtilization shows GPUs idle with no straggler, kernel logs are clean with no Xid/ECC/throttle events, slurm logs show only health-check noise, and CWAgent lacks the nvidia_smi/efa metrics entirely. The EFA fabric attachment itself looks healthy at 8-of-8.

With adjudication complete, the picture is clear: on the B200 training job across both nodes, all 16 GPUs sat completely idle for the entire ~2.3-day run — this was a stall to near-zero, not a gradual throughput decline, and FSx read traffic stayed near-zero the whole time too. I'm ready to finalize this synthesis and move into the mitigation phase.

Looking at storage first as one of the three candidate branches, I can rule it out definitively — FSx never saturated. The one spike in network throughput utilization happened during a one-time dataset-hydration burst back on Aug 26, completely separate from the actual run; during Sep 23–25 itself, FSx showed near-zero reads, almost no client connections, flat free capacity, and low CPU/IOPS on both the metadata and data servers. Since the ~15 GB dataset was hydrated once and then served from client-side page cache, there was never a storage bottleneck here.

Turning to GPUs as the second branch, I'm also ruling that out as a hardware fault — no Xid errors, ECC issues, remapped rows, or thermal/power throttling on either active node across continuous hourly coverage from Sep 23 through Sep 27, and no straggler since all 48 GPUs in the fleet sit uniformly at idle power. Driver version meets the minimum requirement too. The GPUs look idle and waiting rather than degraded, since genuinely faulty hardware would still show elevated power draw from ECC retries or other activity.

For networking, I can't fully rule it out — EFA is fully attached across all interfaces, the security group has the correct self-referencing rules, and both nodes sit in the same subnet and AZ, but a soft NCCL or collective communication issue can't be confirmed or excluded given the available telemetry.

The real issue is that nothing captured whether NCCL actually used EFA versus falling back to TCP or SHM — the debug transport lines, EFA error counters, and Fabric Manager status are all missing because training stdout wasn't shipped and the CWAgent EFA plugin and observability install failed. So the root cause ultimately comes down to a gap in instrumentation rather than a confirmed hardware or network fault.

Storage (FSx) and network provisioning (EFA attachment, security groups, subnet/AZ) are confirmed healthy.
